clue.text: Informed this bit of crossword dessert should be returned

parts.note: the setter points at the thing you are reading: a crossword is made of these

indicators.note: Something returned comes back the way it went, so in an across entry those letters are written in from the right.

parts.note: pud is the British shortening of pudding, the sweet course

explanation.surface: Word going round that the pudding is to be sent back to the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen falls at 5-2, one letter along from the join between the two pieces, so the split the enumeration shows is not the split the wordplay uses.
explanation.definitionFit: To be clued up on a subject is the British idiom for being well informed about it, having the facts to hand.

clue.text: Restrained speed after crashing at the outset

indicators.note: What comes after a thing is written behind it, so the speed named first in the clue is the second piece down.
The outset is the very start, so only the opening letter of the word it follows is taken.

parts.note: the letter CRASHING starts with
haste is speed in the sense of hurrying

explanation.surface: A driver easing off the accelerator after coming to grief in the first corner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Restrained' looks like a past-tense verb reporting what happened to the speed, and it is the adjective doing the defining. The restraint meant has nothing to do with driving.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaste means holding back from indulgence — restrained in appetite, in ornament or in conduct.

clue.text: Seduced academic embraced by a Parisienne

indicators.note: To be embraced is to be held within someone's arms, so this piece sits inside the one named after it.

parts.note: a woman in Paris says une for 'a'
a don is a university teacher, at Oxford and Cambridge especially

explanation.surface: A scholar in the arms of a Parisian woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The French wanted is the feminine article, which is what the -enne ending on 'Parisienne' quietly specifies. The sense of the definition is Victorian, and the surface knows it.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman seduced was said to be undone — ruined, her good name gone — the older sense the clue's romance points at.

clue.text: Curves and dots decorated book jackets

indicators.note: A decorated surface has been worked over until it no longer looks as it did, and letters worked over come out in a new arrangement.

parts.note: ten letters of fodder, with 'and' holding them together

explanation.surface: Book jackets printed all over with a pattern of swirls and spots.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the clue belongs to the same picture, so no seam shows between the letters and the definition. Ten letters is a long shuffle for a Quiptic; the two S's are the way in.
explanation.definitionFit: A dust cover is the loose printed paper wrapper round a hardback, sold as the book's jacket.

clue.text: Cannelloni, perhaps, and where it appears in the dictionary?

definitions.meaning: cannelloni is one named shape out of a very large family of them, which is what 'perhaps' signals

definitions.text: where it appears in the dictionary
definitions.meaning: read as two words this answers the question literally: anything beginning with C is filed beyond the letter A

explanation.surface: Somebody names an Italian dish and wonders whereabouts in the dictionary to find it.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is not a dictionary sense at all but the same five letters split after four, and the question mark is the setter admitting as much.
explanation.definitionFit: Cannelloni is one pasta shape among many, and split after four letters the answer reads 'past A', where every C-word sits alphabetically.

clue.text: Following American, notice a nitpicker

parts.note: f. is the abbreviation for 'following' in an index or a page reference
the US is America, so the two letters stand for American
to spot something is to notice it

explanation.surface: Trailing an American and picking out someone who quibbles over everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' is the printed abbreviation f., as in 'see page 12f.', not the verb the surface offers. Three ordinary pieces in a row, nothing rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A fusspot frets over details everyone else lets pass, which is nitpicking by another name.

clue.text: Like the Bee Gees fan later excited about origin of rock

indicators.note: Letters get excited the way a crowd does, and an excited crowd will not stay in the order it was put in.
What is about something is set around it, so the shuffled letters close over the single letter clued next.

parts.note: eight letters of fodder

indicators.note: An origin is where a thing begins, so only the first letter of the word after it is used.

parts.note: the letter ROCK begins with

explanation.surface: A Bee Gees fan working himself up over where rock music started.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bee Gees were the three Gibb brothers, and their relationship to each other is the entire definition — the disco has nothing to do with it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bee Gees were brothers, so the adjective for the bond between brothers describes what they were to one another.

clue.text: Some players I demand for team

indicators.note: Some of a thing is a part of it lifted out unbroken, which is how these letters are sitting.

parts.note: four consecutive letters spanning both word breaks

explanation.surface: A supporter telling the manager exactly which players he insists on seeing picked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I demand' sounds like the speaker throwing his weight about and is really two of the words the letters run through. Short hidden words hide best across a gap like that.
explanation.definitionFit: A side is a team in British sporting talk — the eleven a captain names on a Saturday.

clue.text: Airborne soldier not bright, welcoming good example

parts.note: a para is a paratrooper, the soldier who arrives by parachute

indicators.note: To welcome somebody is to take them in, so the letters just clued open up and let the next piece sit inside.

parts.note: dim is the everyday word for slow-witted
g stands for good, as on a school report

explanation.surface: A paratrooper who is no genius but takes kindly to being set a good example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not bright' is about wits, not lighting, and 'good example' reads as one phrase when only the first word of it is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A paradigm is the model example of something, the specimen every other case is measured against.

clue.text: Drone reverberating in your Biblical song of lamentation

indicators.note: A sound that reverberates comes back off the walls unsettled and altered, and these letters come back in a different order.

parts.note: thy is the old second-person possessive, the one the Bible and the prayer book use

indicators.note: What is in a thing sits inside it, so the shuffled letters land in the middle of the piece clued next.

parts.note: five letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A droning noise echoing round a church during a reading from scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Your' is the modern form and the archaic one is wanted, which is the whole job of 'Biblical'. The word itself is Greek, from the wailing sung over a body.
explanation.definitionFit: A threnody is a lament composed for the dead, sung or spoken over them in mourning.

clue.text: Attaching a name of the French mountains

indicators.note: To attach is to fasten one thing onto another, so the pieces here are simply written end to end.

parts.note: the clue's own a, taken as a single letter
n. is the abbreviation for name
des is how French says 'of the' in front of a plural

explanation.surface: Fixing a French name onto a range of peaks.
explanation.walkthrough: The French mountains are a decoy: only 'of the' is French, and the range meant runs down South America. The Alps never come into it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Andes are the chain running the length of South America, a plural name for a run of mountains.

clue.text: One offers fake news: spacecraft appearing in series?

indicators.note: Something appearing in a thing has turned up inside it, so the piece before it drops into the middle of the piece after.

parts.note: ser. is the abbreviation for series in a catalogue or a reference list
a lander is the craft that sets down on a moon or a planet

explanation.surface: An invented story about a spacecraft turning up in a television series.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Series' is the catalogue abbreviation ser., not the television kind the surface dangles. The falsehoods meant are spoken ones — put them in print and the word would be libeller.
explanation.definitionFit: A slanderer spreads damaging untruths about people, which is fake news in its oldest and most personal form.

clue.text: Drink ruined winter coat

indicators.note: A ruined thing has lost the shape it had, and these letters lose the order they were given.

parts.note: ten letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A spilt drink has wrecked somebody's winter coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruined' sits between the definition and the letters and could belong to either, which is what keeps it invisible. The answer is a drink in its own right, not merely the half you add to gin.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonic water is the quinine-flavoured fizz sold by the bottle, drunk on its own as well as in a gin.

clue.text: Have dinner, ignoring latest racket

indicators.note: What is ignored is left out, so the letter named straight after it takes no part in the answer.

parts.note: to dine is to have dinner
the latest letter is the last one along, the E at the end of DINE

explanation.surface: Getting on with dinner and paying no attention to the newest fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Latest' means last in the queue rather than most recent, and 'racket' is noise rather than anything you swing. Three-letter answers give you no crossings to argue with.
explanation.definitionFit: A din is a loud unbroken noise — the racket a crowded room makes.

clue.text: Prosecute criminal sequestering a very remote region

indicators.note: A criminal breaks the rules he was given, and letters told to be criminal break out of the order they were given.
To sequester is to shut something away inside, so the shuffled letters close round the letter clued next.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder
the clue's own a, taken as a single letter

explanation.surface: A criminal trial in which somebody is shut away out of reach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very' is the trap: in a crossword it usually hands over a V, and here it belongs to the definition instead. Juries get sequestered, which is why the word reads as courtroom scenery.
explanation.definitionFit: Outer space is everything past the atmosphere, about as remote as a region can be and still have a name.

clue.text: Treated too well, vile underdog will turn nasty

indicators.note: Something that turns nasty has changed into something else, and letters that change come out in a different arrangement.

parts.note: twelve letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A spoiled and unpleasant underdog who is about to show his teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs straight into the fodder as though it were all one sentence about the underdog, so the seam never announces itself. The doubled D and doubled E are the letters to build from.
explanation.definitionFit: A child or a pet overindulged has been given far too much of everything — treated better than was good for it.

clue.text: Tries to block genuine theatre preparation

indicators.note: To block something is to get in its way, so this piece pushes into the middle of the one clued next.

parts.note: real is genuine, in the not-counterfeit sense
a court that tries a case hears it

explanation.surface: Somebody doing their best to obstruct real preparations at the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves borrow stage vocabulary — blocking is the director's word for setting the actors' moves — while the wordplay is courtroom language underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: A rehearsal is the run-through a company does before the audience is let in, the standard preparation for a production.

clue.text: Mike in Ushant, possibly Northern fellow pursuing fox?

indicators.note: What is only possibly so is not fixed, so the letters beside it are free to take some other arrangement.

parts.note: Mike is M in the radio alphabet, alongside Oscar and Tango
six letters of fodder — Ushant is the island off the western tip of Brittany
n. is the abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: A northerner called Mike chasing a fox somewhere off the Breton coast.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is split either side of its own indicator, so 'Northern' has to be pulled back into the letters rather than read as part of the man's description.
explanation.definitionFit: The huntsman is the man in charge of the hounds on a fox hunt, named here by what he is chasing.

clue.text: Notice study — not entirely stupid — as an extra item

indicators.note: Not entirely means stopping short of the whole, so the word it governs gives up its final letter.

parts.note: an ad is a notice placed in a paper
a den is the little room at home you work in
stupid is DUMB, held back from its closing B

explanation.surface: A notice about a piece of research that is not altogether daft.
explanation.walkthrough: The dashes turn 'not entirely stupid' into an aside about the study, which is how an instruction passes for opinion.
explanation.definitionFit: An addendum is matter added at the back of a book or a document, an extra item appended once the main text is set.

clue.text: Led by, and steered, following West? Not impressed

indicators.note: What follows a thing is written after it, so the steering named earlier ends up behind the compass letter.

parts.note: a team under a manager is led by them
w is the compass abbreviation for west
a ship steered by someone has been helmed by them

explanation.surface: A crew who sailed under a skipper named West and came home distinctly unmoved.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark after 'West' is the setter flagging that the word is a compass point cut down to a letter, not a name. Whelmed is the lost middle term the answer was coined against.
explanation.definitionFit: To be underwhelmed is to be left flat by something that promised more, which is exactly failing to be impressed.

clue.text: The German's receiving charge for cloth seller

indicators.note: To receive something is to take it in, so these letters open to admit the piece clued next.

parts.note: der is one of the German words for 'the', and the 's here is only 'is'
a rap is a criminal charge, as in taking the rap for something

explanation.surface: A German landed with the bill from the fabric shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The German' is not a man but the German word for 'the', which the possessive 's disguises by making him the subject of a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A draper is the shopkeeper who sells fabric by the yard, a British high-street trade now nearly extinct.

clue.text: Rescue rock group crossing river

indicators.note: To cross a river is to lie over it from one bank to the other, so these letters span the ones clued next.

parts.note: REM are the American band behind Losing My Religion
the Dee is a British river, one in Wales and another in Aberdeenshire

explanation.surface: A band picking their way across a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rescue rock' reads as one phrase and the definition is only the first word of it. Three letters and a vague 'river' is a crossword staple — Dee, Exe, Ouse, Po — so the crossings decide which.
explanation.definitionFit: To redeem is to buy something back or save it from being lost, which is rescuing it.

clue.text: Prison sentence eliminating male bond

indicators.note: To eliminate is to get rid of, so the letter named after it is struck out of the word before it.

parts.note: time is the word for a stretch inside — doing time
m is the abbreviation for male, and it is the letter eliminated

explanation.surface: A jail term that does away with a man's attachments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bond' pulls towards chains and cells, where the surface wants it, and means an attachment between people instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie is a bond between people — the link of family or loyalty that holds them to each other.

clue.text: A sister wildly tucking into dessert in cake shop

indicators.note: Anything done wildly keeps no order, so the letters beside it come out rearranged.

parts.note: a pie comes round as the sweet course

indicators.note: To tuck into something is to get right inside it, so the shuffled letters land in the middle of the piece clued next.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder, the article included

explanation.surface: A sister demolishing a pudding with great enthusiasm in a cake shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Tucking into a dessert is precisely what you would be doing in the place defined, so the instruction hides inside the scene it describes.
explanation.definitionFit: A patisserie is the shop that bakes and sells fine cakes and pastries, French in its name and its stock alike.

clue.text: One pawn caught in trap? That's not very competent

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: Whatever is caught in a trap is held inside it, so this letter drops into the middle of the piece clued before it.

parts.note: a net is what traps a fish or a bird
p is the chess notation for a pawn

explanation.surface: A lone pawn blundering into a trap on the board.
explanation.walkthrough: Chess supplies the pawn and the trap, so the surface holds together while the three pieces come from three unrelated places. 'That's' is doing nothing but making the clue a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Inept is the blunt word for what 'not very competent' says politely: clumsy, unskilled, making a mess of it.

clue.text: Insubstantial object, with bottom missing

indicators.note: What is missing is not there, so the letter named just before it never reaches the grid.

parts.note: an object is a thing
in a down entry the bottom letter is the final one, the G of THING

explanation.surface: A flimsy article that has lost its base.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma makes 'object' look like more of the description when it is the word the letters come from. Bottom means last only because the entry runs downwards; across, it would say nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something thin has no weight or body to it — a thin excuse is as insubstantial as a thin sheet of paper.

clue.text: Steamed ahead? Steam ahead, dropping an article clumsily

indicators.note: What is dropped is let fall and left behind, so the letter named after it goes before anything else happens.
Work done clumsily comes out misshapen, and letters handled clumsily come out in the wrong order.

parts.note: ten letters, before anything is taken out
a is the indefinite article, and it is the letter let go

explanation.surface: Full steam ahead, with a newspaper piece clumsily let fall along the way.
explanation.walkthrough: Definition and fodder are the same two words twice over, one tense apart, which is the joke and also what makes the seam so hard to find. 'An article' could be a, an or the; only losing a single A leaves nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To make haste is to hurry, and a ship that steamed ahead did just that — got moving at speed.

clue.text: Liberal politician getting stuck into beer

indicators.note: To get stuck into something is to plunge straight in, so this piece goes inside the one clued after it.

parts.note: ale is beer
an MP is a Member of Parliament, the standard British politician

explanation.surface: A Liberal MP settling down to a pint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal politician' reads as a party label, helped by the capital that starts the clue, and a Liberal in a crossword usually hands over an L. Here the word is the definition entire.
explanation.definitionFit: A liberal helping and an ample one are the same size: generous, more than enough to go round.

clue.text: Trivial pit running short with no aluminium around

indicators.note: What goes around a thing closes on both sides of it, so these two pieces end up either side of the letters between them.
To run short is to stop before the end, so the word before it surrenders its last letter.

parts.note: the clue's own no, taken as two letters
a pit is a mine, cut off before its final E
Al is the chemical symbol for aluminium

explanation.surface: A mine closing early because there is no aluminium left in the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running short' does to the word what running short of ore does to a pit, so the instruction passes as part of the story. The outer piece is split, half before the middle and half after.
explanation.definitionFit: A nominal fee or a nominal role exists in name only, so slight that it hardly counts.

clue.text: Source of metal retained by those people in principle

indicators.note: What is retained is kept within, so the piece before it is held inside the piece clued after.

parts.note: them is the pronoun for those people
ore is the rock that metal is got out of

explanation.surface: A group of people holding on to a seam of metal, at least in theory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Source of' looks like the standard instruction to take a first letter and is a plain synonym instead, which is the one thing worth checking before counting letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A theorem is a general truth proved by argument in mathematics, which is what a principle is in looser talk.
